title: Why does Greenland look so big on a map?
description: On a Mercator map, places near the poles look larger than they really are relative to the rest of the world. Here’s why.

sections.title: A flat map has to stretch something
sections.html:
Greenland can look enormous on a wall map. On a globe, its size relative to places near the equator is much less dramatic.

The difference comes from the map projection: the method used to show Earth’s curved surface on a flat page. A Mercator projection stretches areas more and more towards the poles. Greenland sits far to the north, so its size is exaggerated.

This does not happen in the same way on every rectangular map. Different projections preserve different features, such as area, local shape or direction.

sections.title: Which map should you use?
sections.html:
For comparing sizes, use a globe or an equal-area map. Equal-area projections keep relative areas correct, although shapes may look unfamiliar.

Other projections are useful for other purposes. As the US Geological Survey explains, there is no single best projection for every task. A map that helps with navigation may be a poor choice for comparing how much land two places cover.

sections.title: Compare a globe with a Mercator map
sections.html:
Find Greenland and a place near the equator on both. Compare their apparent sizes. Which looks larger on the flat map than it does on the globe?

Now try an equal-area world map. The outlines may look different, but the size comparison should be easier to trust.

Does an equal-area map also preserve every country’s shape?

No. Keeping relative areas correct and preserving local shapes are different goals. A flat world map cannot preserve everything at once.
